Regularity for axisymmetric Navier-Stokes with an Euler length

Peter Constantin Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08540 Email address: const@math.princeton.edu URL: https://web.math.princeton.edu/˜const/ , Mihaela Ignatova Address: Department of Mathematics, Temple University, Philadelphia, PA 19122 Email address: ignatova@temple.edu URL: https://sites.temple.edu/ignatova/ and Vlad Vicol Address: Department of Mathematics, Courant Institute, New York University, New York, NY, 10012 Email address: vicol@cims.nyu.edu URL: https://cims.nyu.edu/˜vicol/
Abstract.

We prove local regularity for axisymmetric suitable weak solutions of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, which are smooth before the terminal time t=0t=0, and satisfy Type II pointwise bounds at a vanishing length scale ℓ⁡(t)\ell(t). We say ℓ⁡(t)\ell(t) is an Euler length if it is non-increasing, satisfies a doubling condition, and if ℓ⁡(t)→0\ell(t)\to 0 and (−t)/ℓ​(t)2→0(-t)/\ell(t)^{2}\to 0 as t→0−t\to 0^{-}. This includes power laws ℓ⁡(t)=(−t)γ\ell(t)=(-t)^{\gamma} with 0<γ<1/20<\gamma<1/2, and logarithmic enlargements of the parabolic length. Our main result shows that local bounds of the type |u⁡(⋅,t)|≤C​ℓ​(t)/(−t)|u(\cdot,t)|\leq C\ell(t)/(-t) and |∇2u​(⋅,t)|≤C/((−t)​ℓ​(t))|\nabla^{2}u(\cdot,t)|\leq C/((-t)\ell(t)) for all t∈(−1,0)t\in(-1,0) imply regularity. The proof adapts the circulation and potential-vorticity argument of our earlier paper [4] to ancient limits obtained from the rescaled vorticity system by zooming in. We show that the second derivative a priori assumption may be replaced by a Hölder bound on the azimuthal vorticity and a corresponding bound on its potential vorticity.

Key words and phrases: 
Navier-Stokes equations, local regularity, axial symmetry, ancient vorticity limits.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 35Q30; Secondary 35B44, 35Q31

1. Introduction

Whether an axisymmetric finite energy solution of the unforced 3D Navier-Stokes equations, arising from smooth and decaying initial data, can develop a finite time singularity remains an open problem.

In this paper, we consider the 3D Navier-Stokes equations without external forcing

(1.1a) ∂tu+(u⋅∇)u−Δu+∇π=0,\displaystyle\partial_{t}u+(u\cdot\nabla)u-\Delta u+\nabla\pi=0\,,
(1.1b) div​u=0,\displaystyle\mathrm{div\,}u=0\,,

where u:Q→ℝ3u\colon Q\to\mathbb{R}^{3} is the velocity, π:Q→ℝ\pi\colon Q\to\mathbb{R} is the pressure, and Q=B⁡(1)×(−1,0)Q=B(1)\times(-1,0) is an open unit parabolic cylinder.11 1 Here and throughout this paper, we use the notation B⁡(ρ)={x∈ℝ3:|x|<ρ}B(\rho)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:|x|<\rho\} and Q⁡(ρ)=B⁡(ρ)×(−ρ2,0)Q(\rho)=B(\rho)\times(-\rho^{2},0). Throughout the paper we take (u,π)(u,\pi) to be a suitable weak solution of (1.1) in the sense of Caffarelli, Kohn, and Nirenberg [1], with π∈L3/2​(Q)\pi\in L^{3/2}(Q), which is smooth on compact subsets of QQ. We assume no regularity at time t=0t=0. Moreover, we assume throughout the paper that the solution (u,π)(u,\pi) of (1.1) is axisymmetric about the zz-axis. With x=(x′,z)x=(x^{\prime},z), r=|x′|r=|x^{\prime}|, and the usual cylindrical frame (er,eθ,ez)(e_{r},e_{\theta},e_{z}), we set

u=ur​er+uθ​eθ+uz​ez=b+uθ​eθ,u=u_{r}e_{r}+u_{\theta}e_{\theta}+u_{z}e_{z}=b+u_{\theta}e_{\theta}\,,

where ur,uθ,uzu_{r},u_{\theta},u_{z} depend only on (r,z,t)(r,z,t). We denote by bb the meridional velocity.

1.1. Main result

In order to state our main result, we introduce:

Definition 1.1 (Euler length).

A continuous function ℓ:(−1,0)→(0,∞)\ell\colon(-1,0)\to(0,\infty) is called an Euler length if it is non-increasing, it satisfies the doubling property

(1.2a) ℓ(2t)≤Dℓ(t),for all t∈(−1/2,0),\ell(2t)\leq D\ell(t)\,,\qquad\mbox{for all }t\in(-1/2,0)\,,
for a suitable constant D∈[1,∞)D\in[1,\infty), it asymptotically vanishes
(1.2b) limt↑0ℓ⁡(t)=0,\lim_{t\uparrow 0}\ell(t)=0\,,
and it satisfies
(1.2c) limt↑0(−t)ℓ​(t)2=0.\lim_{t\uparrow 0}\frac{(-t)}{\ell(t)^{2}}=0.

The term “Euler length” is motivated in part by the requirement (1.2c) that the viscosity coefficient under Euler rescaling vanishes asymptotically, so formally the Euler behavior emerges in the limit.

Examples of Euler lengths are ℓ⁡(t)=(−t)γ\ell(t)=(-t)^{\gamma} for γ∈(0,1/2)\gamma\in(0,1/2) and ℓ⁡(t)=(−t)1/2​(log⁡(e/(−t)))a\ell(t)=(-t)^{1/2}(\log(e/(-t)))^{a} with 0<a≤1/20<a\leq 1/2.

Recall that the point (0,0)(0,0) is called regular if

(1.3) ess​supQ⁡(ρ)⁡|u|​<∞for some ​ρ>​0.\displaystyle\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{Q(\rho)}|u|<\infty\quad\mbox{for some }\rho>0\,.

More generally, for x0∈B⁡(1)x_{0}\in B(1) the point (x0,0)(x_{0},0) is called regular if (1.3) holds with Q⁡(ρ)Q(\rho) replaced by B⁡(x0,ρ)×(−ρ2,0)⊂QB(x_{0},\rho)\times(-\rho^{2},0)\subset Q, and singular otherwise. The simplest way to state the main result of this paper is:

Theorem 1.2 (Local regularity under Type II bounds at an Euler length).

Let (u,π)(u,\pi) be a suitable weak solution of (1.1) in QQ, which is smooth on compact subsets of QQ, and is axisymmetric. Let ℓ=ℓ⁡(t)\ell=\ell(t) be an Euler length, in the sense of Definition 1.1. Suppose that there exist constants C0,C2>0C_{0},C_{2}>0 such that

(1.4) ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))≤C0​ℓ⁡(t)(−t),‖∇2u​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))≤C2​1(−t)​ℓ​(t),\displaystyle\left\|u(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))}\leq C_{0}\frac{\ell(t)}{(-t)}\,,\qquad\left\|\nabla^{2}u(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))}\leq C_{2}\frac{1}{(-t)\ell(t)}\,,

for all t∈(−1,0)t\in(-1,0). Then, (0,0)(0,0) is a regular point.

Remark 1.3.

The following comments on the hypotheses of Theorem 1.2 are in order:

  • (a)

    For the power law ℓ⁡(t)=(−t)γ\ell(t)=(-t)^{\gamma} with γ∈(0,1/2)\gamma\in(0,1/2), the two Type II bounds in (1.4) say that the natural self-similar Euler rescaling U⁡(y,t):=(−t)1−γ​u​((−t)γ​y,t)U(y,t):=(-t)^{1-\gamma}u((-t)^{\gamma}y,t) satisfies ‖U⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞≤C0\left\|U(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{0} and ‖∇y2​U​(⋅,t)‖L∞≤C2\left\|\nabla^{2}_{y}U(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{2}, where the L∞L^{\infty} norm is taken on the expanding ball B⁡((−t)−γ)B((-t)^{-\gamma}).

  • (b)

    If the first bound in (1.4) holds with the parabolic length scale ℓ⁡(t)=(−t)1/2\ell(t)=(-t)^{1/2}, then we have a standard Type I bound. In that case, regularity is known due to the works of Chen, Strain, Tsai, and Yau [2, 3], Koch, Nadirashvili, Seregin, and Šverák [9], or Seregin and Šverák [21].

  • (c)

    The Type II assumption made in (1.4) is more restrictive than necessary, and the bounds on the second derivative can be relaxed. In Section 5 we prove the same regularity result under weaker hypotheses: a Hölder seminorm bound on the azimuthal vorticity ωθ=∂zur−∂ruz\omega_{\theta}=\partial_{z}u_{r}-\partial_{r}u_{z} and a supremum bound for the potential vorticity Ω=ωθ/r\Omega=\omega_{\theta}/r, at the Euler length. Precisely, in Theorem 5.1 we assume, for some 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1, the velocity L∞L^{\infty} bound in (1.4) together with

    [ωθ​(⋅,t)]Cα​(B​(1))≤Cα(−t)​ℓ​(t)α,‖Ω⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))≤CH(−t)​ℓ​(t),\displaystyle[\omega_{\theta}(\cdot,t)]_{C^{\alpha}(B(1))}\leq\frac{C_{\alpha}}{(-t)\ell(t)^{\alpha}}\,,\qquad\left\|\Omega(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))}\leq\frac{C_{H}}{(-t)\ell(t)}\,,

    for some constants Cα,CH>0C_{\alpha},C_{H}>0.

  • (d)

    The same weakening of regularity assumptions from Theorem 5.1 also applies to the main result of [4, Section 4]. Theorem 4.5 in [4] excludes nontrivial C2C^{2} axisymmetric globally self-similar Euler profiles with similarity exponent γ<1/2\gamma<1/2 which obey the natural far-field bounds [4, (3.8)]. In Proposition 6.1 we extend this result to continuous self-similar profiles which vanish at the origin and are sublinear at infinity, whose azimuthal vorticity is locally Hölder continuous, and whose potential vorticity is locally bounded; no far-field decay beyond sublinearity is assumed.

1.2. Prior results

In the absence of swirl, global regularity for the axisymmetric 3D Navier-Stokes equations was established by Ladyzhenskaya [10] and by Ukhovskii and Yudovich [26].

In the presence of swirl, the regularity of axisymmetric solutions to 3D Navier-Stokes has been established under the additional hypothesis of a Type I bound, an assumption which is invariant under parabolic scaling. Chen, Strain, Yau, and Tsai [2] proved regularity of the solution at t=0t=0 assuming the pointwise bound |u|≤C(r2−t)−1/2|u|\leq C(r^{2}-t)^{-1/2}. Chen, Strain, Tsai, and Yau [3] and Koch, Nadirashvili, Seregin, and Šverák [9] proved regularity assuming that r​|u|≤Cr|u|\leq C. Seregin and Šverák [21] imposed a temporal Type I bound on the meridional velocity alone: |b|≤C(−t)−1/2|b|\leq C(-t)^{-1/2}. All of these proofs rely on the structure of the equations satisfied by the circulation and by the potential vorticity Ω=ωθ/r\Omega=\omega_{\theta}/r. We refer to the book of Tsai [25, Chapter 10] for a detailed account of the many conditional regularity results for solutions of 3D axisymmetric Navier-Stokes.

Escauriaza, Seregin, and Šverák [6, Theorem 1.4] proved the regularity of suitable weak solutions which are bounded in the scale-invariant norm Lt∞​Lx3L^{\infty}_{t}L^{3}_{x}; their argument is by contradiction and gives no quantitative bound. Tao [24] made this result quantitative for classical solutions on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and obtained a quantitative lower bound, of triple logarithmic type, for the blowup rate of the L3L^{3} norm at a finite time singularity, along a sequence of times approaching that singularity. Subsequently, Palasek [14] replaced the triple logarithm by a double logarithm, for the weighted critical norms ‖r1−3/q​u‖Lq\|r^{1-3/q}u\|_{L^{q}}, both for axisymmetric solutions with q∈(2,3]q\in(2,3] and for solutions without any symmetry with q∈(3,∞)q\in(3,\infty). Ożański and Palasek [13] then bounded every derivative of an axisymmetric solution by a double exponential of its weak L3L^{3} norm. Seregin [15] proved that at a singular axis point the three scale-invariant local energy quantities arising in the theory of partial regularity all have an infinite upper limit, so that an axisymmetric singularity must be Type II also in the local-energy sense. Seregin also formulated Type II blowup scenarios through such weighted scale-invariant quantities and studied them in [16, 17, 18, 19].

The argument in this paper is inspired by the axisymmetric Euler profile theorem that we have established in our earlier work [4, Theorem 4.5]. We adapt the potential-vorticity transport along backward meridional trajectories, from the proof of [4, Theorem 4.5], to ancient limits of the rescaled vorticity system; here the circulation is eliminated by the rescaling instead. The type of argument employed here, in which we zoom in at a sequence of points and times where a desired bound fails, and apply a rigidity statement to the resulting ancient limit, is the one through which Type I singularities were excluded previously [9, 21]. We emphasize that in this paper we do not assume a self-similar ansatz for the solution.

1.3. Main ideas of the proof

The proof of Theorem 1.2 has two parts. First, we show that the gradient of the meridional velocity becomes small compared with its scale-invariant bound, namely

(1.5) limt↑0(−t)​‖∇b​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B⁡(ρ0))=0on a fixed ball ​B​(ρ0),0<ρ0<1.\displaystyle\lim_{t\uparrow 0}(-t)\left\|\nabla b(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(\rho_{0}))}=0\quad\mbox{on a fixed ball }B(\rho_{0})\,,\quad 0<\rho_{0}<1\,.

Second, we show that (1.5) implies regularity at (0,0)(0,0).

For the first part we argue by contradiction. If (1.5) fails, we zoom in at the length ℓ⁡(t)\ell(t) along a sequence of times and points at which (−t)​|∇b|(-t)|\nabla b| stays bounded away from zero, and we ask what the limit satisfies. In the context of Type II weighted scale-invariant bounds on shrinking cylinders, this approach was considered by Seregin [16, 17, 18, 19]. At a length larger than the parabolic one the pressure is not controlled after the zoom, so we pass to the limit in the vorticity equation rather than in the momentum one. Two facts make the limit tractable. First, the circulation Γ\Gamma is bounded on a fixed ball, by partial regularity and the maximum principle for (2.3). A bounded circulation is subcritical for the rescaling by an Euler length: after the zoom-in, it is bounded by a multiple of (−t)/ℓ​(t)2(-t)/\ell(t)^{2}, which tends to zero as t↑0t\uparrow 0. The swirl of every limit therefore vanishes, and with it the source ∂z(uθ2/r2)\partial_{z}(u_{\theta}^{2}/r^{2}) of the potential vorticity equation (2.5) vanishes as well. For the ancient limits arising in his Type II scenarios, Seregin [17, Section 2] observed in the same way that the swirl vanishes. Since the swirl source vanishes, the limiting potential vorticity is transported by a locally bounded, divergence free field which is Lipschitz in space with constant C1/|τ|C_{1}/|\tau| (see (3.3)); here τ∈(−∞,−1]\tau\in(-\infty,-1] is the rescaled time of the ancient limit of the vorticity system. The second is that along the backward characteristics of that limiting divergence free field the potential vorticity is constant, and at time τ\tau it inherits the bound C/|τ|C/|\tau| from the hypotheses (1.4). Therefore the limiting azimuthal vorticity vanishes at τ=−1\tau=-1: in the finite-axis case through the potential vorticity, and in the receding-axis case by transporting the azimuthal vorticity itself. This is the content of Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3. The limiting meridional velocity at τ=−1\tau=-1 is then curl-free, divergence-free, and bounded on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, hence constant. On the other hand, the selection of the contradiction sequence forces the gradient of the limiting meridional velocity to be nonzero at one point. This contradiction proves (1.5); see Proposition 3.1.

For the second part, we apply the maximum principle in the swirl equation (2.3) to (−t)η​uθ(-t)^{\eta}u_{\theta} and obtain |uθ|≤Cη​(−t)−η|u_{\theta}|\leq C_{\eta}(-t)^{-\eta} on a smaller fixed ball, for every η>0\eta>0. A localized enstrophy estimate then gives u∈Lt4​Lx6u\in L^{4}_{t}L^{6}_{x} on a fixed parabolic cylinder with top (0,0)(0,0). Regularity then follows from the localized version of the Ladyzhenskaya-Prodi-Serrin criterion; see Section 4.

Remark 1.4 (What is special about axisymmetry?).

The exclusion of Type I singularities is not known without the assumption of axisymmetry, and we do not know how to prove Theorem 1.2 without it when ℓ⁡(t)=(−t)γ\ell(t)=(-t)^{\gamma} with 2/5≤γ<1/22/5\leq\gamma<1/2, or when ℓ\ell is a logarithmic enlargement of the parabolic length. What this rotational invariance supplies is not merely the reduction to the variables (r,z)(r,z), which leaves vortex stretching intact, but the two identities (2.3) and (2.5). The circulation obeys a drift-diffusion equation with no zeroth order term, so that it satisfies a maximum principle. Moreover, the circulation scales like viscosity: an axisymmetric solution carries an a priori bounded critical quantity, and we know of none for (1.1) in the general setting of flows on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. The potential vorticity obeys a transport-diffusion equation whose only other term is the swirl source ∂z(Γ2/r4)\partial_{z}(\Gamma^{2}/r^{4}); without swirl this is the global regularity of [10, 26], and with swirl the Liouville theorems of [9] are proved through the same two equations.

Remark 1.5 (Euler profiles and the viscous question).

Consider a putative 3D Navier-Stokes singularity in the absence of external forces, constructed from a self-similar Euler singularity by treating the viscosity as an asymptotic perturbation. With the singular time at t=0t=0, the similarity ansatz u⁡(x,t)=(−t)γ−1​U​(x/(−t)γ,−log⁡(−t))u(x,t)=(-t)^{\gamma-1}U(x/(-t)^{\gamma},-\log(-t)) carries the viscosity coefficient (−t)1−2​γ(-t)^{1-2\gamma}, which tends to zero as t↑0t\uparrow 0 precisely when γ<1/2\gamma<1/2. These are the power laws of Definition 1.1. In essence, Theorem 1.2 shows what such a construction has to give up in the axisymmetric setting: the viscous solution cannot remain bounded in C2C^{2} in similarity variables, on a fixed ball in the original variables, no matter what profile it is meant to approach at the blowup time.

Organization of the paper

In Section 2 we record the axisymmetric identities, a regular annulus obtained from partial regularity, and a transport lemma. In Section 3 we prove the two ancient-limit lemmas and deduce Proposition 3.1 from them. In Section 4 we give the local regularity conclusion and the logarithmic examples. In Sections 5 and 6 we prove the regularity statements for Navier-Stokes solutions and for Euler self-similar profiles under weaker assumptions.

2. Axisymmetric identities and auxiliary results

In this section we record the axisymmetric identities (see e.g. [25, Chapter 10]) and a few technical lemmas which will be used later in the proof. We decompose the velocity field into its meridional and swirl components

(2.1) u=b+w,b:=ur​er+uz​ez,w:=uθ​eθ,u=b+w\,,\qquad b:=u_{r}e_{r}+u_{z}e_{z}\,,\qquad w:=u_{\theta}e_{\theta}\,,

and note that both bb and ww are divergence free. For the azimuthal component of the vorticity we denote

ωθ:=(curl​u)θ=∂zur−∂ruz,Ω:=ωθr,\omega_{\theta}:=(\mathrm{curl\,}u)_{\theta}=\partial_{z}u_{r}-\partial_{r}u_{z}\,,\qquad\Omega:=\frac{\omega_{\theta}}{r}\,,

and note that

curl​b=ωθ​eθ.\mathrm{curl\,}b=\omega_{\theta}e_{\theta}\,.

We refer to Ω\Omega as the potential vorticity: denoting ω=curl​u\omega=\mathrm{curl\,}u we have Ω=ω⋅∇θ\Omega=\omega\cdot\nabla\theta, which is Ertel’s potential vorticity associated with the azimuthal angle θ\theta, and θ\theta is materially conserved precisely when the swirl vanishes.

For a vector field FF we write |∇F||\nabla F| to denote the Euclidean norm of the Jacobian matrix, so that |curl​F|≤2​|∇F||\mathrm{curl\,}F|\leq\sqrt{2}\,|\nabla F|. Lipschitz and Hölder seminorms of rotation-invariant scalars are taken in the Euclidean distance.

2.1. Axisymmetric identities

For smooth axisymmetric solutions, the meridional projection of (1.1) is given by

(2.2a) ∂tb+div⁡(b⊗b)+∇π\displaystyle\partial_{t}b+\mathrm{div\,}(b\otimes b)+\nabla\pi =Δ​b−div⁡(w⊗w),\displaystyle=\Delta b-\mathrm{div\,}(w\otimes w)\,,
(2.2b) div​b\displaystyle\mathrm{div\,}b =0,\displaystyle=0\,,
with the swirl velocity contributing the Reynolds stress
(2.2c) div⁡(w⊗w)=−uθ2r​er.\displaystyle\mathrm{div\,}(w\otimes w)=-\frac{u_{\theta}^{2}}{r}\,e_{r}\,.

The swirl velocity uθu_{\theta} and the circulation Γ=r​uθ\Gamma=ru_{\theta} satisfy

(2.3) ∂tuθ+b⋅∇uθ+urruθ=(Δ−1r2)uθ,∂tΓ+b⋅∇Γ=(Δ−2r∂r)Γ.\displaystyle\partial_{t}u_{\theta}+b\cdot\nabla u_{\theta}+\frac{u_{r}}{r}u_{\theta}=\Big(\Delta-\frac{1}{r^{2}}\Big)u_{\theta}\,,\qquad\partial_{t}\Gamma+b\cdot\nabla\Gamma=\Big(\Delta-\frac{2}{r}\partial_{r}\Big)\Gamma\,.

The azimuthal vorticity obeys

(2.4) ∂tωθ+b⋅∇ωθ=(Δ−1r2)​ωθ+urr​ωθ+1r​∂z(uθ2).\displaystyle\partial_{t}\omega_{\theta}+b\cdot\nabla\omega_{\theta}=\Big(\Delta-\frac{1}{r^{2}}\Big)\omega_{\theta}+\frac{u_{r}}{r}\,\omega_{\theta}+\frac{1}{r}\,\partial_{z}\big(u_{\theta}^{2}\big)\,.

Dividing (2.4) by rr, and using r−1(Δ−r−2)(rg)=(Δ+2r−1∂r)gr^{-1}(\Delta-r^{-2})(rg)=(\Delta+2r^{-1}\partial_{r})g for axisymmetric scalars gg, we obtain

(2.5) ∂tΩ+b⋅∇Ω=(Δ+2r∂r)Ω+∂z(uθ2r2).\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Omega+b\cdot\nabla\Omega=\Big(\Delta+\frac{2}{r}\,\partial_{r}\Big)\Omega+\partial_{z}\Big(\frac{u_{\theta}^{2}}{r^{2}}\Big)\,.

We recall the standard fact that near the axis of symmetry, the components of a smooth axisymmetric vector field uu take the form ur=r​a​(r2,z,t)u_{r}=r\,a(r^{2},z,t), uθ=r​c​(r2,z,t)u_{\theta}=r\,c(r^{2},z,t), uz=d⁡(r2,z,t)u_{z}=d(r^{2},z,t) for some smooth functions a,c,da,c,d; thus, Ω\Omega and uθ2/r2u_{\theta}^{2}/r^{2} extend smoothly to the axis, and (2.5) holds on the whole domain.

The following lemma records bounds for Ω\Omega in terms of the Hessian of uu.

Lemma 2.1 (Pointwise bounds across the axis).

Let uu be a smooth axisymmetric vector field, not necessarily a solution of (1.1), defined on an open axisymmetric set 𝒰⊂ℝ3\mathcal{U}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} which meets the axis of symmetry.

  1. (a)

    We have |ωθ/r|≤2​|∇2u|\big|\omega_{\theta}/r\big|\leq\sqrt{2}\,|\nabla^{2}u| at every point of 𝒰\mathcal{U} off the axis, where ωθ=∂zur−∂ruz\omega_{\theta}=\partial_{z}u_{r}-\partial_{r}u_{z} and |∇2u||\nabla^{2}u| denotes the Euclidean norm of the full tensor (∂i∂juk)i,j,k(\partial_{i}\partial_{j}u_{k})_{i,j,k}.

  2. (b)

    With meridional part b=ur​er+uz​ezb=u_{r}e_{r}+u_{z}e_{z} and swirl part w=uθ​eθw=u_{\theta}e_{\theta}, we have |∇ju|2=|∇jb|2+|∇jw|2|\nabla^{j}u|^{2}=|\nabla^{j}b|^{2}+|\nabla^{j}w|^{2} pointwise in 𝒰\mathcal{U} for j=0,1,2j=0,1,2, and |∇ωθ|≤2​|∇2u||\nabla\omega_{\theta}|\leq\sqrt{2}\,|\nabla^{2}u| off the axis. In particular, ωθ\omega_{\theta}, extended by zero to the axis, is Lipschitz on every open convex set K⊆𝒰K\subseteq\mathcal{U}, with constant 2​‖∇2u‖L∞​(K)\sqrt{2}\|\nabla^{2}u\|_{L^{\infty}(K)}.

Proof of Lemma 2.1.

Every quantity in the lemma is invariant under rotations about the axis; thus, it suffices to work at a point x0=(x1,0,z)∈𝒰x_{0}=(x_{1},0,z)\in\mathcal{U}, with x1=r>0x_{1}=r>0. In Cartesian components, an axisymmetric field F=Fr​er+Fθ​eθ+Fz​ezF=F_{r}e_{r}+F_{\theta}e_{\theta}+F_{z}e_{z}, with Fr,Fθ,FzF_{r},F_{\theta},F_{z} functions of (r,z)(r,z), reads

(2.6) F1=Fr​x1r−Fθ​x2r,F2=Fr​x2r+Fθ​x1r,Fz=Fz​(r,z).\displaystyle F_{1}=F_{r}\,\frac{x_{1}}{r}-F_{\theta}\,\frac{x_{2}}{r}\,,\qquad F_{2}=F_{r}\,\frac{x_{2}}{r}+F_{\theta}\,\frac{x_{1}}{r}\,,\qquad F_{z}=F_{z}(r,z)\,.

Differentiating (2.6) and evaluating at x0x_{0}, we obtain

(2.7) ∂2F1​(x0)=−Fθr​(x0).\displaystyle\partial_{2}F_{1}(x_{0})=-\frac{F_{\theta}}{r}(x_{0})\,.

In order to prove item (a), we apply (2.7) to the smooth axisymmetric field F=ω:=curl​uF=\omega:=\mathrm{curl\,}u. 2.3. Transport

In our proof we argue that certain limits of the vorticity obtained by zooming in solve in the weak sense a transport equation whose drift is itself only a weak-∗* limit. For this purpose, we recall that for a divergence free drift which is bounded and Lipschitz in space on compact sets, with a Lipschitz constant which is locally integrable in time, a continuous distributional solution of the transport equation is constant along the characteristics of the drift. We state here a version adapted to our setting:

Lemma 2.3 (Constancy along characteristics).

Let 𝒰⊂ℝ3×(−∞,−1]\mathcal{U}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}\times(-\infty,-1] be relatively open. Let B:𝒰→ℝ3B\colon\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{R}^{3} be bounded on compact sets, measurable in τ\tau, Lipschitz in yy on compact sets with a Lipschitz constant λ⁡(τ)\lambda(\tau) which is locally integrable in time, and divergence free in yy for almost every τ\tau. Let Λ:𝒰→ℝ\Lambda\colon\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{R} be a continuous weak solution of the transport equation ∂τΛ+divy​(B​Λ)=0\partial_{\tau}\Lambda+\mathrm{div\,}_{\!\!y}(B\Lambda)=0 in the interior of 𝒰\mathcal{U}.22 2 That is, ∫𝒰Λ⁡(∂τφ+B⋅∇φ)​𝑑y​𝑑τ=0\int_{\mathcal{U}}\Lambda\big(\partial_{\tau}\varphi+B\cdot\nabla\varphi\big)\,dy\,d\tau=0 for every φ∈C0∞​(int​𝒰)\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathrm{int}\,\mathcal{U}). Let X:(−∞,−1]→ℝ3X\colon(-\infty,-1]\to\mathbb{R}^{3} be absolutely continuous on compact subintervals, with X˙​(τ)=B​(X​(τ),τ)\dot{X}(\tau)=B(X(\tau),\tau) for almost every τ\tau, and suppose that {(X⁡(τ),τ):τ0≤τ≤−1}\{(X(\tau),\tau)\colon\tau_{0}\leq\tau\leq-1\} is a compact subset of 𝒰\mathcal{U} for every τ0<−1\tau_{0}<-1. Then τ↦Λ⁡(X⁡(τ),τ)\tau\mapsto\Lambda(X(\tau),\tau) is constant on (−∞,−1](-\infty,-1].

The proof of the above result is standard: with the notation of Lemma 2.3, it mollifies the solution in space, bounds the commutator of DiPerna and Lions [5, Lemma II.1] uniformly on compact sets by a constant multiple of λ⁡(τ)\lambda(\tau) times the modulus of continuity of Λ\Lambda at the mollification scale (this uses the continuity of Λ\Lambda), and integrates the mollified equation in time along XX. This commutator bound is written out, in a stationary setting, in Step 3 of the proof of Proposition 6.1. We omit further details.

3. Ancient limits at the Euler length

In this section we construct ancient limits at the Euler length, and use them to prove that on a fixed ball the meridional gradient becomes small compared with the scale-invariant bound C1/(−t)C_{1}/(-t), which our hypotheses give directly, see (3.3) below. In Section 4 we show that this smallness implies regularity, and thus Theorem 1.2.

Proposition 3.1 (Smallness of the meridional gradient).

Let ℓ\ell be an Euler length, in the sense of Definition 1.1, and assume that the bounds (1.4) hold for all t∈(−1,0)t\in(-1,0). Then

(3.1) limt↑0(−t)​‖∇b​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1/2))=0.\displaystyle\lim_{t\uparrow 0}(-t)\left\|\nabla b(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1/2))}=0\,.

We prove Proposition 3.1 by contradiction. If (3.1) fails, there are times tn↑0t_{n}\uparrow 0 and points xn∈B⁡(1/2)x_{n}\in B(1/2) at which (−tn)​|∇b​(xn,tn)|(-t_{n})|\nabla b(x_{n},t_{n})| stays bounded away from zero. We zoom in at time tnt_{n} about a base point built from xnx_{n}, in space using the Euler length ℓ⁡(tn)\ell(t_{n}), and in time using |tn||t_{n}| itself. Our goal is to analyze the ancient limits of the rescaled solution. A priori these limits are not known to solve the Euler equations in their momentum form: at a length larger than the parabolic one the pressure is not controlled after the zoom-in, so that we cannot pass to the limit in the momentum equation. Instead, we pass to the limit in the vorticity equation.

Two facts make analyzing the limit tractable, and both were described in Section 1.3: by Lemma 2.2 the circulation is bounded on a fixed ball, and a bounded circulation is subcritical for this rescaling by (1.2c), so that the swirl of every limit vanishes together with the swirl source ∂z(uθ2/r2)\partial_{z}(u_{\theta}^{2}/r^{2}) of (2.5); and Lemma 2.3 makes the limiting vorticity constant along the backward characteristics of the limiting drift, so that the bound C/|τ|C/|\tau| it inherits from (1.4) forces it to vanish. The two eliminations, first of the circulation and then of the potential vorticity, each along backward meridional trajectories, are the main idea of the proof of [4, Theorem 4.5]. Here the circulation is eliminated instead by the rescaling, as observed for the ancient limits of an Euler scaling by Seregin [17, Section 2]. What is new here is that the potential vorticity is transported along the trajectories of a time-dependent field which is only a weak-∗* limit, for which the transport equation holds only weakly and only off the axis (we keep these trajectories off the axis through a quantitative lower bound on their distance to it), and that the potential vorticity vanishes because of the bound C/|τ|C/|\tau| inherited from (1.4), rather than because of an exponential weight as in [4].

The main result of the construction is the pair of Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3: along a subsequence, the rescaled azimuthal vorticity converges locally uniformly to a limit which vanishes at τ=−1\tau=-1, and the rescaled meridional velocity at τ=−1\tau=-1 converges in C1C^{1} on compact sets to a field which is curl free, divergence free, and bounded on all of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. Thus each component is bounded and harmonic, hence constant by Liouville’s theorem. The selection of the points xnx_{n} forces the gradient of this limit to be bounded away from zero at one point, which provides the desired contradiction. In Section 3.1 we define the zoom-in and record the bounds it inherits from (1.4), in Section 3.2 we prove the two lemmas, and in Section 3.3 we select the sequences tnt_{n} and xnx_{n} and complete the proof of Proposition 3.1.

3.2. Two ancient-limit lemmas

Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 below are at the heart of the limit argument. They differ in whether the axis is present in the limit, and in which scalar we transport; everything else is common to them.

Lemma 3.2 (Ancient limits, the axis present).

Let tnt_{n}, ana_{n}, and the fields (3.5) be as in Section 3.1, with every ana_{n} lying on the axis of symmetry. Define 𝒪:=ℝ3×(−∞,−1]\mathcal{O}:=\mathbb{R}^{3}\times(-\infty,-1], and let L¯:(−∞,−1]→[1,∞)\bar{L}\colon(-\infty,-1]\to[1,\infty) be non-decreasing in |τ||\tau|, bounded on bounded sets, and such that

(3.10) lim supn→∞sup−T≤τ≤−1Ln​(τ)L¯​(τ)≤1for every ​T>1.\displaystyle\limsup_{n\to\infty}\,\sup_{-T\leq\tau\leq-1}\frac{L_{n}(\tau)}{\bar{L}(\tau)}\leq 1\qquad\mbox{for every }T>1\,.

Then, there exists a continuous Θ:𝒪→ℝ\Theta\colon\mathcal{O}\to\mathbb{R}, with |Θ⁡(y,τ)|≤2​C1/|τ||\Theta(y,\tau)|\leq\sqrt{2}\,C_{1}/|\tau| on 𝒪\mathcal{O}, and

(3.11) Θ⁡(⋅,−1)=0on ​ℝ3,\displaystyle\Theta(\cdot,-1)=0\qquad\mbox{on }\mathbb{R}^{3}\,,

such that after passing to a subsequence we have

(3.12) Θn⟶Θuniformly on compact subsets of ​𝒪.\displaystyle\Theta_{n}\longrightarrow\Theta\qquad\mbox{uniformly on compact subsets of }\mathcal{O}\,.

Moreover, along a further subsequence, Bn​(⋅,−1)→B∗B_{n}(\cdot,-1)\to B^{*} in C1C^{1} on compact subsets of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, where B∗B^{*} is divergence free, curl free, and bounded by C0C_{0}, so that each of its components is harmonic.

Lemma 3.3 (Ancient limits, the axis receding).

Let tnt_{n}, ana_{n}, and the fields (3.5) be as in Section 3.1, with an′=(rn,0)a_{n}^{\prime}=(r_{n},0) and dn=rn/ℓn→∞d_{n}=r_{n}/\ell_{n}\to\infty. Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} and L¯\bar{L} be as in Lemma 3.2. Then the conclusions of Lemma 3.2 all hold.

Proof of Lemma 3.2.

For convenience, we break down the argument into five steps.

Step 1: compactness of the azimuthal vorticity. Since curl​b=ωθ​eθ\mathrm{curl\,}b=\omega_{\theta}e_{\theta}, by (3.5) we have that

curl​Bn​(y,τ)=Θn​(y,τ)​eθ​(y)\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}(y,\tau)=\Theta_{n}(y,\tau)\,e_{\theta}(y)

for all yy off the axis. Here we have used that eθ​(an+ℓn​y)=eθ​(y)e_{\theta}(a_{n}+\ell_{n}y)=e_{\theta}(y) because ana_{n} lies on the axis. For yy on the axis, both Θn\Theta_{n} and curl​Bn\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n} vanish, and we deduce that

|curl​Bn|=|Θn||\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}|=|\Theta_{n}|

holds at every point of 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}. Since |curl​Bn|≤2​|∇Bn||\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}|\leq\sqrt{2}\,|\nabla B_{n}|, the bound (3.8c) gives |curl​Bn|≤2​C1/|τ|≤2​C1|\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}|\leq\sqrt{2}C_{1}/|\tau|\leq\sqrt{2}C_{1} on every compact subset of 𝒪\mathcal{O}, for all nn large depending on the set. The bound (3.8b) makes curl​Bn\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n} Lipschitz in yy, with constant 2​C2\sqrt{2}C_{2}, on every closed ball contained in 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}. By Lemma 2.1(b) applied to u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) on the convex axisymmetric ball B⁡(1)B(1), and using the change of variables in (3.5), the scalars Θn​(⋅,τ)\Theta_{n}(\cdot,\tau) are Lipschitz on 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} with the same constant 2​C2\sqrt{2}C_{2}. We use both Lipschitz bounds only on the closed balls appearing in the next paragraph.

Taking the curl of (3.6), we obtain for every y¯∈ℝ3\bar{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, ρ>0\rho>0, τa<τb≤−1\tau_{a}<\tau_{b}\leq-1, 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, and all nn large depending on these,

Here W−2,p​(B​(y¯,ρ))W^{-2,p}(B(\bar{y},\rho)) denotes the dual of W02,p′​(B⁡(y¯,ρ))W^{2,p^{\prime}}_{0}(B(\bar{y},\rho)), and we used the fact that the quadratic terms are two derivatives of tensor fields bounded by (3.8a), the viscous term is εn​Δ​curl​Bn\varepsilon_{n}\Delta\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n} with curl​Bn\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n} and εn\varepsilon_{n} bounded, and the pressure term is gone. Since the embedding C0,1​(B⁡(y¯,ρ)¯)↪C0​(B⁡(y¯,ρ)¯)C^{0,1}(\overline{B(\bar{y},\rho)})\hookrightarrow C^{0}(\overline{B(\bar{y},\rho)}) is compact and C0​(B⁡(y¯,ρ)¯)C^{0}(\overline{B(\bar{y},\rho)}) embeds continuously and injectively into W−2,p​(B​(y¯,ρ))W^{-2,p}(B(\bar{y},\rho)), a standard compactness argument gives, for every η>0\eta>0, a constant CηC_{\eta} with

‖F‖C0​(B⁡(y¯,ρ)¯)≤η​‖F‖C0,1​(B⁡(y¯,ρ)¯)+Cη​‖F‖W−2,p​(B​(y¯,ρ))for all ​F∈C0,1​(B⁡(y¯,ρ)¯).\left\|F\right\|_{C^{0}(\overline{B(\bar{y},\rho)})}\leq\eta\left\|F\right\|_{C^{0,1}(\overline{B(\bar{y},\rho)})}+C_{\eta}\left\|F\right\|_{W^{-2,p}(B(\bar{y},\rho))}\qquad\mbox{for all }F\in C^{0,1}(\overline{B(\bar{y},\rho)})\,.

Applying this bound to F=curl​Bn​(τ)−curl​Bn​(τ′)F=\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}(\tau)-\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}(\tau^{\prime}), using (3.8b), (3.8c), and the previous estimate for ∂τcurl​Bn\partial_{\tau}\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}, we find that the maps τ↦curl​Bn​(τ)\tau\mapsto\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}(\tau) are equicontinuous with values in C0​(B⁡(y¯,ρ)¯)C^{0}(\overline{B(\bar{y},\rho)}). The unit vector eθ​(an+ℓn​y)e_{\theta}(a_{n}+\ell_{n}y) does not depend on τ\tau, so that the scalars Θn\Theta_{n} are equicontinuous in τ\tau as well, and they are equicontinuous in yy by the Lipschitz bound recorded in the previous paragraph. Every compact subset of 𝒪\mathcal{O} lies in one such product, being bounded in yy and in τ\tau, and 𝒪\mathcal{O} is the union of the products B⁡(0,k)¯×[−k,−1]\overline{B(0,k)}\times[-k,-1] with k≥1k\geq 1; applying the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem on each of these and extracting diagonally, we obtain (3.12), where Θ\Theta is continuous on 𝒪\mathcal{O}. The bound |Θ⁡(y,τ)|≤2​C1/|τ||\Theta(y,\tau)|\leq\sqrt{2}\,C_{1}/|\tau| is inherited from (3.8c).

The quotients Ωn=Θn/|y′|\Omega_{n}=\Theta_{n}/|y^{\prime}| converge uniformly on compact subsets of 𝒪∩{y′≠0}\mathcal{O}\cap\{y^{\prime}\neq 0\} to Ω∞:=Θ/|y′|\Omega_{\infty}:=\Theta/|y^{\prime}|, and by (3.8d) we have

|Ω∞​(y,τ)|≤2​C2|τ|.|\Omega_{\infty}(y,\tau)|\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}C_{2}}{|\tau|}\,.

Step 2: the limiting meridional velocity. By (3.8a) and (3.8c), the fields BnB_{n} and ∇Bn\nabla B_{n} are bounded on every compact subset of 𝒪\mathcal{O}. After a further diagonal extraction we have Bn⇀BB_{n}\rightharpoonup B and ∇Bn⇀∇B\nabla B_{n}\rightharpoonup\nabla B weakly-∗* in L∞L^{\infty} on every such set, with ∇B\nabla B the distributional spatial gradient of BB. The limit satisfies div​B=0\mathrm{div\,}B=0, curl​B=Θ​eθ\mathrm{curl\,}B=\Theta\,e_{\theta}, and due to (3.8c), (3.8a), and (3.10) it obeys

Since BB is defined only up to a null set, for almost every τ\tau we replace B⁡(⋅,τ)B(\cdot,\tau) by its continuous representative, which is divergence free, Lipschitz on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} with constant C1/|τ|C_{1}/|\tau|, and bounded by C0​L¯​(τ)/|τ|C_{0}\bar{L}(\tau)/|\tau| at every y∈ℝ3y\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. On the exceptional null set of times we set B⁡(⋅,τ)=0B(\cdot,\tau)=0. The resulting field is continuous in yy at every τ\tau by construction, and measurable in τ\tau at every yy. The Carathéodory solutions of X˙​(τ)=B​(X​(τ),τ)\dot{X}(\tau)=B(X(\tau),\tau), that is, the absolutely continuous XX which satisfy the equation in integral form, do not see the exceptional set. The fields BnB_{n} are axisymmetric and swirl free, and thus so is BB. Since BB is continuous in yy, its radial component BrB_{r} vanishes on the axis, and the Lipschitz bound gives |Br​(y,τ)|≤C1​|y′|/|τ||B_{r}(y,\tau)|\leq C_{1}|y^{\prime}|/|\tau|.

(3.14) ∂τΩn+div(BnΩn)=εn(Δ+2|y′|∂|y′|)Ωn+∂z(|Zn|2|y′|2)on {y∈𝒟n,y′≠0}.\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}\Omega_{n}+\mathrm{div\,}\Bigl(B_{n}\,\Omega_{n}\Bigr)=\varepsilon_{n}\Big(\Delta+\frac{2}{|y^{\prime}|}\partial_{|y^{\prime}|}\Big)\Omega_{n}+\partial_{z}\Big(\frac{|Z_{n}|^{2}}{|y^{\prime}|^{2}}\Big)\qquad\mbox{on }\{y\in\mathcal{D}_{n},\ y^{\prime}\neq 0\}\,.

We fix φ∈C0∞\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{0} compactly supported in the interior of 𝒪∩{y′≠0}\mathcal{O}\cap\{y^{\prime}\neq 0\} and test (3.14) against φ\varphi. For all large enough nn, we have supp⁡(φ)⊂𝒟n♭\mathrm{supp\,}(\varphi)\subset\mathcal{D}_{n}^{\flat}. for every φ∈C0∞\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{0} compactly supported in the interior of 𝒪∩{y′≠0}\mathcal{O}\cap\{y^{\prime}\neq 0\}. In (3.15) the transported function Ω∞\Omega_{\infty} is continuous and bounded on its domain, and the velocity is bounded on compact subsets of 𝒪\mathcal{O}, divergence free, measurable in time, and Lipschitz in space on compact sets.

Step 4: characteristics and the vanishing of the limit vorticity. We fix a point y0∈ℝ3y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} off the axis. Since B⁡(⋅,τ)B(\cdot,\tau) is Lipschitz on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} with constant C1/|τ|C_{1}/|\tau| and is bounded by C0​L¯​(τ)/|τ|C_{0}\bar{L}(\tau)/|\tau|, the equation X˙​(τ)=B​(X​(τ),τ)\dot{X}(\tau)=B(X(\tau),\tau) with X⁡(−1)=y0X(-1)=y_{0} has a unique solution XX on (−∞,−1](-\infty,-1], absolutely continuous on compact subintervals. |Ω∞​(y0,−1)|=limτ→−∞|Ω∞​(X⁡(τ),τ)|≤limτ→−∞2​C2|τ|=0,|\Omega_{\infty}(y_{0},-1)|=\lim_{\tau\to-\infty}|\Omega_{\infty}(X(\tau),\tau)|\leq\lim_{\tau\to-\infty}\frac{\sqrt{2}C_{2}}{|\tau|}=0\,,

Being a weak-∗* limit in L∞L^{\infty} of the sequence BnB_{n} (see Step 2), the field BB is determined only up to null sets of 𝒪\mathcal{O}, and the slice {τ=−1}\{\tau=-1\} is one. Proof of Lemma 3.3.

We follow the five steps of the proof of Lemma 3.2, and we only record the necessary changes.

Step 1: compactness of the azimuthal vorticity. Since curl​b=ωθ​eθ\mathrm{curl\,}b=\omega_{\theta}e_{\theta}, by (3.5) we now have

curl​Bn​(y,τ)=Θn​(y,τ)​eθ​(an+ℓn​y)\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}(y,\tau)=\Theta_{n}(y,\tau)\,e_{\theta}(a_{n}+\ell_{n}y)

wherever Rn​(y)=|an′+ℓn​y′|/ℓn>0R_{n}(y)=|a_{n}^{\prime}+\ell_{n}y^{\prime}|/\ell_{n}>0. Since ana_{n} does not lie on the symmetry axis we cannot equate eθ​(an+ℓn​y)e_{\theta}(a_{n}+\ell_{n}y) with eθ​(y)e_{\theta}(y); however, because dn→∞d_{n}\to\infty and an′=(rn,0)a_{n}^{\prime}=(r_{n},0) we have eθ​(an+ℓn​y)→e2e_{\theta}(a_{n}+\ell_{n}y)\to e_{2} uniformly on compact subsets of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. Since Rn​(y)≥rn/ℓn−|y′|≥dn−|y|R_{n}(y)\geq r_{n}/\ell_{n}-|y^{\prime}|\geq d_{n}-|y|, we deduce that |curl​Bn|=|Θn||\mathrm{curl\,}B_{n}|=|\Theta_{n}| on every compact subset of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, for all nn large depending on the set. 3.3. Proof of Proposition 3.1

Since ℓ⁡(t)→0\ell(t)\to 0, we may fix T1∈(0,1]T_{1}\in(0,1] for which (3.2) holds, so that the fields and the bounds of Section 3.1 are available. In particular, (3.3) shows that supt∈(−T1,0)(−t)​‖∇b​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1/2))≤C1\sup_{t\in(-T_{1},0)}(-t)\left\|\nabla b(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1/2))}\leq C_{1}.

Suppose by contradiction that (3.1) fails. Then there exist c0>0c_{0}>0, times tn↑0t_{n}\uparrow 0 with tn∈(−T1,0)t_{n}\in(-T_{1},0), and points xn∈B⁡(1/2)x_{n}\in B(1/2) with

(3.19) (−tn)​|∇b​(xn,tn)|≥c0.\displaystyle(-t_{n})|\nabla b(x_{n},t_{n})|\geq c_{0}\,.

By rotational invariance we may without loss of generality take xn′=(rn,0)x_{n}^{\prime}=(r_{n},0). Recall that ℓn=ℓ⁡(tn)\ell_{n}=\ell(t_{n}). After passing to a subsequence, either rn/ℓnr_{n}/\ell_{n} is bounded (finite-axis), or rn/ℓn→∞r_{n}/\ell_{n}\to\infty (receding-axis). These are the two configurations discussed in Section 3.1, and we choose the points ana_{n} from (3.5) accordingly: in the finite-axis configuration we define an:=(0,0,xn⋅ez)a_{n}:=(0,0,x_{n}\cdot e_{z}), while in the receding-axis configuration we define an:=xna_{n}:=x_{n}. In both cases |an|≤|xn|<12|a_{n}|\leq|x_{n}|<\frac{1}{2}, and the image yn∗:=(xn−an)/ℓny_{n}^{*}:=(x_{n}-a_{n})/\ell_{n} of xnx_{n} under the zoom-in from (3.5) is (rn/ℓn,0,0)(r_{n}/\ell_{n},0,0) and (0,0,0)(0,0,0) respectively, hence bounded.

In terms of the doubling constant D≥1D\geq 1 from (1.2a), we define L¯:(−∞,−1]→[1,∞)\bar{L}\colon(-\infty,-1]\to[1,\infty) by

L¯​(τ):=D⌈log2⁡|τ|⌉.\displaystyle\bar{L}(\tau):=D^{\lceil\log_{2}|\tau|\rceil}\,.

This function is non-decreasing in |τ||\tau| and satisfies L¯​(τ)≤CT\bar{L}(\tau)\leq C_{T} for −T≤τ≤−1-T\leq\tau\leq-1, with CTC_{T} as in (3.7). By monotonicity and doubling, Ln​(τ)≤DkL_{n}(\tau)\leq D^{k} for all τ∈[−2k,−2k−1)∩[−T,−1]\tau\in[-2^{k},-2^{k-1})\cap[-T,-1] and 0≤k≤⌈log2⁡T⌉0\leq k\leq\lceil\log_{2}T\rceil, for all large nn (depending on TT). Therefore, Ln≤L¯L_{n}\leq\bar{L} on [−T,−1][-T,-1] for every T>1T>1, and all nn large enough depending on TT. Thus, we have verified assumption (3.10).

We apply Lemma 3.2 in the finite-axis configuration and Lemma 3.3 in the receding-axis configuration. In both cases, along a subsequence Bn​(⋅,−1)→B∗B_{n}(\cdot,-1)\to B^{*} in C1C^{1} on compact subsets of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, with each component of B∗B^{*} being harmonic. Since yn∗y_{n}^{*} is bounded, after passing to a further subsequence we have yn∗→y∗y_{n}^{*}\to y^{*}. Differentiating (3.5), we obtain ∇Bn(yn∗,−1)=(−tn)∇b(xn,tn)\nabla B_{n}(y_{n}^{*},-1)=(-t_{n})\nabla b(x_{n},t_{n}), and since ∇Bn​(⋅,−1)→∇B∗\nabla B_{n}(\cdot,-1)\to\nabla B^{*} uniformly on compact sets, passing to the limit in (3.19) yields |∇B∗​(y∗)|≥c0|\nabla B^{*}(y^{*})|\geq c_{0}. 4. The local regularity conclusion

In this section we use the asymptotic vanishing statement (1.5) (which for ρ0=1/2\rho_{0}=1/2 is (3.1)) to prove regularity of the flow on a smaller fixed ball, which completes the proof of Theorem 1.2.

Proposition 4.1 (Smallness of (−t)​‖∇b​(⋅,t)‖L∞(-t)\left\|\nabla b(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}} implies regularity).

Suppose that (1.5) holds for some ρ0∈(0,1)\rho_{0}\in(0,1). Then (0,0)(0,0) is a regular point.

We fix a regular annulus for uu inside B⁡(ρ0)B(\rho_{0}), as in Lemma 2.2; we also fix the time t0t_{0} and the radii R−<R+R_{-}<R_{+} this lemma supplies, together with an R∗∈(R−,R+)R_{*}\in(R_{-},R_{+}). Proof of Theorem 1.2.

By Proposition 3.1, the bounds (1.4) give (3.1), which is (1.5) with ρ0=1/2\rho_{0}=1/2, and Proposition 4.1 makes (0,0)(0,0) a regular point. ∎

Note that Theorem 1.2 gives regularity not just for ℓ⁡(t)=(−t)γ\ell(t)=(-t)^{\gamma} with γ∈(0,1/2)\gamma\in(0,1/2), but also for power laws with a logarithmic correction.

Corollary 4.2 (Local power laws and logarithmic corrections).

Let (u,π)(u,\pi) be as in Theorem 1.2, with (1.4) being replaced by the two local bounds

(4.4) ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))≤C​(−t)γ−1​(log⁡e(−t))a,‖∇2u​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))≤C​(−t)−1−γ​(log⁡e(−t))−a,\displaystyle\left\|u(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))}\leq C(-t)^{\gamma-1}\Big(\log\frac{e}{(-t)}\Big)^{a}\,,\qquad\left\|\nabla^{2}u(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))}\leq C(-t)^{-1-\gamma}\Big(\log\frac{e}{(-t)}\Big)^{-a}\,,

5. Weaker vorticity assumptions

The second derivative bound in Theorem 1.2 is more than the proof uses. In this section we state the form of the theorem which the proof actually gives, with a Hölder seminorm of the azimuthal vorticity and a bound on the potential vorticity in place of ∇2u\nabla^{2}u. The only additional ingredient we need is an interior div-curl estimate.

Theorem 5.1 (Local regularity under matched vorticity bounds).

Let 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1. Let (u,π)(u,\pi) and ℓ\ell be as in Theorem 1.2, with (1.4) being replaced by the assumptions

(5.1) ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))≤C0​ℓ⁡(t)(−t),[ωθ​(⋅,t)]Cα​(B​(1))≤Cα(−t)​ℓ​(t)α,‖Ω⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))≤CH(−t)​ℓ​(t),\displaystyle\left\|u(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))}\leq C_{0}\frac{\ell(t)}{(-t)}\,,\quad[\omega_{\theta}(\cdot,t)]_{C^{\alpha}(B(1))}\leq\frac{C_{\alpha}}{(-t)\ell(t)^{\alpha}}\,,\quad\left\|\Omega(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))}\leq\frac{C_{H}}{(-t)\ell(t)}\,,

Then (0,0)(0,0) is a regular point. When α=1\alpha=1 the third bound follows from the second, and may be omitted.

For the power law ℓ⁡(t)=(−t)γ\ell(t)=(-t)^{\gamma}, the three upper bounds in (5.1) are (−t)γ−1(-t)^{\gamma-1}, (−t)−1−α​γ(-t)^{-1-\alpha\gamma}, and (−t)−1−γ(-t)^{-1-\gamma}. That is, the rescaled field U⁡(y,t)=(−t)1−γ​u​((−t)γ​y,t)U(y,t)=(-t)^{1-\gamma}u((-t)^{\gamma}y,t) is bounded, has CαC^{\alpha} azimuthal vorticity, and has bounded potential vorticity on the expanding ball B⁡(1/(−t)γ)B(1/(-t)^{\gamma}). Lemma 2.1(b) turns the Hessian bound in (1.4) into the second bound in (5.1) at α=1\alpha=1, and Lemma 2.1(a) turns it into the third. Theorem 1.2 is therefore the case α=1\alpha=1 of Theorem 5.1.

5.1. Interior div-curl estimates

The bounds in (5.1) control the velocity and the Hölder seminorm of the azimuthal vorticity. The following lemma converts them into a gradient bound, and after the zoom-in into a uniform C1,βC^{1,\beta} bound. Part (a) passes from the scalar ωθ\omega_{\theta} to the vector ωθ​eθ\omega_{\theta}e_{\theta}, and part (b) records the interior Schauder estimates for the div-curl system, as used here.

Indeed, the Hessian bound enters the proofs of the two lemmas in Step 1 and Step 5 only: Steps 2, 3, and 4 use, besides the hypotheses of the two lemmas, only the bounds (3.8a), (3.8c), (3.8d), and (3.8e), the vanishing of εn\varepsilon_{n}, and the conclusions of Step 1.

6. Sublinear Euler profiles under weaker regularity

In this section we carry out, for the self-similar Euler profiles of [4, Section 4], the weakening of regularity hypotheses announced in Remark 1.3(d). In Section 4 of our previous paper [4], we considered axisymmetric, globally self-similar solutions of the 3D Euler equations, with self-similar profile UU and similarity exponent γ>0\gamma>0. Constantin, Ignatova, and Vicol [4, Theorem 4.5] proved that γ≥12\gamma\geq\frac{1}{2} for every nonzero C2C^{2} profile satisfying U⁡(0)=0U(0)=0, sublinearity at infinity, and the far-field bounds

|U(y)|≤C|y|⟨y⟩−1/γ,|∇U(y)|+|curlU(y)|≤C⟨y⟩−1/γ.|U(y)|\leq C|y|\langle y\rangle^{-1/\gamma},\qquad|\nabla U(y)|+|\mathrm{curl\,}U(y)|\leq C\langle y\rangle^{-1/\gamma}.

That paper also fixes the spatial units by the normalization ‖∇2U‖L∞=1\|\nabla^{2}U\|_{L^{\infty}}=1. The normalization does not enter the argument below. Here we retain U⁡(0)=0U(0)=0, continuity, sublinearity, local Hölder regularity of the azimuthal vorticity, and local boundedness of the potential vorticity, but impose no far-field decay beyond sublinearity. We use the pressure-free weak form of the self-similar Euler equation (1−γ)​U+γ​y⋅∇U+U⋅∇U+∇P=0(1-\gamma)U+\gamma y\cdot\nabla U+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla P=0. The identity y⋅∇U=div⁡(y⊗U)−3​Uy\cdot\nabla U=\mathrm{div\,}(y\otimes U)-3U gives (6.1) below.

Proposition 6.1 (Sublinear self-similar Euler profiles).

Let γ>0\gamma>0 and let U∈C⁡(ℝ3,ℝ3)U\in C(\mathbb{R}^{3};\mathbb{R}^{3}) be axisymmetric, with div​U=0\mathrm{div\,}U=0 in 𝒟′​(ℝ3)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), U⁡(0)=0U(0)=0, |U⁡(y)|/|y|→0|U(y)|/|y|\to 0 as |y|→∞|y|\to\infty, and

(6.1) ∫ℝ3((1−4γ)U⋅Ξ−γ(y⊗U):∇Ξ−(U⊗U):∇Ξ)dy=0,\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\Big((1-4\gamma)\,U\cdot\Xi-\gamma\,(y\otimes U):\nabla\Xi-(U\otimes U):\nabla\Xi\Big)\,dy=0\,,

for all Ξ∈C0∞​(ℝ3,ℝ3)\Xi\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{3};\mathbb{R}^{3}) with div​Ξ=0\mathrm{div\,}\Xi=0. Let U=bU+Uθ​eθU=b_{U}+U_{\theta}e_{\theta}, with bU=Ur​er+Uz​ezb_{U}=U_{r}e_{r}+U_{z}e_{z}, be the decomposition of UU in the cylindrical frame of the variable yy, where r=|y′|r=|y^{\prime}|. Assume that curl​bU=ωθ​eθ\mathrm{curl\,}b_{U}=\omega_{\theta}e_{\theta} in 𝒟′​(ℝ3)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), where ωθ\omega_{\theta} is an axisymmetric scalar which vanishes on the axis and belongs to Cloc0,α​(ℝ3)C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) for some α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1]. Also assume that the potential vorticity ωθ/r\omega_{\theta}/r is bounded on B(ρ)∩{r>0}B(\rho)\cap\{r>0\} for every ρ>0\rho>0; this is automatic when α=1\alpha=1. If U≢0U\not\equiv 0, then γ≥12\gamma\geq\frac{1}{2}. If Uθ≡0U_{\theta}\equiv 0, then U≡0U\equiv 0 for every γ>0\gamma>0.

Proof of Proposition 6.1.

The proof is carried out in six steps.

Step 1: regularity of the meridional part. Since a continuous axisymmetric field is parallel to eze_{z} on the axis, UrU_{r} and UθU_{\theta} vanish there, and bUb_{U} is continuous on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. The identity div⁡(Uθ​eθ)=0\mathrm{div\,}(U_{\theta}e_{\theta})=0 holds in 𝒟′​(ℝ3)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3}): away from the axis it follows from the cylindrical divergence formula, while integration over the angular variable and the identity (Uθ​eθ)⋅er=0(U_{\theta}e_{\theta})\cdot e_{r}=0 exclude an axis contribution. Hence div​bU=0\mathrm{div\,}b_{U}=0 in 𝒟′​(ℝ3)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3}).

We fix ρ>0\rho>0, and for 0<ε≤ρ/20<\varepsilon\leq\rho/2 set bε=bU∗ηεb_{\varepsilon}=b_{U}*\eta_{\varepsilon}, where η\eta is a radial mollifier supported in B⁡(1)B(1). Radial convolution preserves rotation equivariance and reflection symmetry across planes containing the axis. Thus bεb_{\varepsilon} is smooth, axisymmetric, and meridional, with div​bε=0\mathrm{div\,}b_{\varepsilon}=0 and curl​bε=(ωθ​eθ)∗ηε\mathrm{curl\,}b_{\varepsilon}=(\omega_{\theta}e_{\theta})*\eta_{\varepsilon}. By (5.2),

[curl​bε]Cα​(B​(ρ/2))≤3​[ωθ]Cα​(B​(ρ)),‖bε‖L∞​(B​(ρ/2))≤‖bU‖L∞​(B​(ρ)).[\mathrm{curl\,}b_{\varepsilon}]_{C^{\alpha}(B(\rho/2))}\leq 3[\omega_{\theta}]_{C^{\alpha}(B(\rho))},\qquad\left\|b_{\varepsilon}\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(\rho/2))}\leq\left\|b_{U}\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(\rho))}.

The bound (5.4) on B⁡(ρ/2)B(\rho/2) therefore bounds bεb_{\varepsilon} in C1,β​(B​(ρ/4))C^{1,\beta}(B(\rho/4)) uniformly in ε\varepsilon, for every β<α\beta<\alpha. For a fixed β<α\beta<\alpha, we apply this statement with an exponent strictly between β\beta and α\alpha. Since bε→bUb_{\varepsilon}\to b_{U} uniformly on compact sets, compactness gives bU∈Cloc1,β​(ℝ3)b_{U}\in C^{1,\beta}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) and bε→bUb_{\varepsilon}\to b_{U} in C1C^{1} on compact sets. In particular, V:=γ​y+bUV:=\gamma y+b_{U} is locally Lipschitz, with div​V=3​γ\mathrm{div\,}V=3\gamma.

Step 2: characteristics. Since VV is locally Lipschitz, the equation Y˙=V⁡(Y)\dot{Y}=V(Y) has unique solutions. By Step 1, Ur=0U_{r}=0 on the axis, so that VV is parallel to eze_{z} there, the axis is invariant, and, by uniqueness, a solution which starts off the axis stays off it. By sublinearity we may fix R♭R_{\flat} with |U⁡(y)|≤γ2​|y||U(y)|\leq\frac{\gamma}{2}|y| for |y|≥R♭|y|\geq R_{\flat}; since |bU|≤|U||b_{U}|\leq|U|, we then have dd​τ​|Y|2=2​γ​|Y|2+2​Y⋅bU​(Y)≥γ​|Y|2\frac{d}{d\tau}|Y|^{2}=2\gamma|Y|^{2}+2Y\cdot b_{U}(Y)\geq\gamma|Y|^{2} whenever |Y|≥R♭|Y|\geq R_{\flat}, so that |Y⁡(τ)|≤max⁡{|Y⁡(0)|,R♭}|Y(\tau)|\leq\max\{|Y(0)|,R_{\flat}\} for τ≤0\tau\leq 0. The standard continuation criterion for locally Lipschitz ordinary differential equations now shows that the backward characteristic starting at a point y0y_{0} off the axis exists on (−∞,0](-\infty,0], stays in the compact set K0:=B⁡(max⁡{|y0|,R♭})¯K_{0}:=\overline{B(\max\{|y_{0}|,R_{\flat}\})}, and stays off the axis.

Step 3: a stationary form of Lemma 2.3. Let ℰ⊂ℝ3\mathcal{E}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} be open, V:ℰ→ℝ3V\colon\mathcal{E}\to\mathbb{R}^{3} locally Lipschitz with div​V=c\mathrm{div\,}V=c, f∈C⁡(ℰ)f\in C(\mathcal{E}), κ∈ℝ\kappa\in\mathbb{R}, and

(6.2) ∫ℰf⁡(κ​ψ−V⋅∇ψ)​𝑑y=0for all ​ψ∈C0∞​(ℰ).\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{E}}f\,\big(\kappa\psi-V\cdot\nabla\psi\big)\,dy=0\qquad\mbox{for all }\psi\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathcal{E})\,.

If Y:[τ0,τ1]→ℰY\colon[\tau_{0},\tau_{1}]\to\mathcal{E} solves Y˙=V⁡(Y)\dot{Y}=V(Y), then eμ​τ​f​(Y⁡(τ))e^{\mu\tau}f(Y(\tau)) is constant. In order to prove this fact, we let N⊂ℰN\subset\mathcal{E} be a compact neighborhood of Y⁡([τ0,τ1])Y([\tau_{0},\tau_{1}]), we take δ<dist⁡(N,ℰ∁)\delta<\mathrm{dist}(N,\mathcal{E}^{\complement}), and we set fδ=f∗ηδf^{\delta}=f*\eta_{\delta} on NN. V⋅∇fδ+μ​fδ=∫(f⁡(ζ)−f⁡(y))​(V⁡(y)−V⁡(ζ))⋅(∇ηδ)​(y−ζ)​𝑑ζ+c⁡(fδ−f)=:𝖾δ.V\cdot\nabla f^{\delta}+\mu f^{\delta}=\int\big(f(\zeta)-f(y)\big)\big(V(y)-V(\zeta)\big)\cdot(\nabla\eta_{\delta})(y-\zeta)\,d\zeta+c\,(f^{\delta}-f)=:\mathsf{e}_{\delta}\,.

The error term 𝖾δ\mathsf{e}_{\delta} may be directly bounded as |𝖾δ|≤C​ν​(δ)​(LN+|c|)|\mathsf{e}_{\delta}|\leq C\,\nu(\delta)\,(L_{N}+|c|), where ν\nu is the modulus of continuity of ff, and LNL_{N} is the Lipschitz constant of VV, both on the closed δ\delta-neighborhood of NN, which is a compact subset of ℰ\mathcal{E}. We shall also use this statement when the scalar identity is initially known only for axisymmetric test functions. Disclaimer on the use of AI systems

Publicly available versions of Claude (Opus 5 and Fable 5.1, within Claude Code) and ChatGPT (Sol and Astra, within Codex) were used in the preparation of this manuscript. These systems were given access to our paper [4] (which was written without the use of AI systems), from which the core idea of the proof is taken, and to an early draft of this manuscript, written entirely by the authors, which contained the whole proof at the level of an eight-page sketch. Claude and ChatGPT were used to fill in the proofs of routine lemmas and arguments in that draft, to perform an extended bibliographic search, and to produce the TikZ figure. Over the course of two extended sessions of Claude Code and Codex, the manuscript was then polished, in its exposition and in the verification of its mathematical computations, under the close guidance and supervision of the authors. Every suggestion, computation, and reference produced by these systems was independently verified and, where necessary, corrected or reformulated by the authors, who take full responsibility for the manuscript as it is presently written.
